g1-emuA.text: In this context, this document needs to be read with the awareness that the legalization of psychedelic substances for regulated use has advanced significantly in certain jurisdictions since this document was published. A number of psilocybin service centers have been licensed and opened to the public under regulatory guidance in the state of Oregon beginning in 2023, a regulated system for natural medicines has been created and is licensing individuals to work with psychedelics in the state of Colorado beginning in 2025, and the Medical Psilocybin Act was passed in the state of New Mexico in 2025. Additionally, in Australia, since 2023, psychiatrists have been able to apply for authorization to prescribe psilocybin and MDMA for a limited number of conditions. As a result, some of the literature that has been cited in this document may not reflect the current state of affairs in the communities in which it was published.

g1-emuB.text: Psychedelic legalization is moving quickly, and many communities’ educational literature has not kept pace. In 2023, Oregon began opening licensed psilocybin service centers. In 2025, Colorado launched a new regulated natural medicine system and began the licensing process. New Mexico passed its Medical Psilocybin Act in 2025. Since 2023, psychiatrists in Australia can prescribe psilocybin and MDMA in limited amounts to treat certain conditions.

g2-emuA.text:
The other thing it tends to draw in are the kinds of people who like the revelations but not the follow-through. It’s great to have all these ceremonies and lore, but if they don’t translate into practical day-to-day life, then the community structure just becomes another way to avoid the mundane tasks that need to be done.

And yes, I do think there can be good use for it in a communal setting. Psychedelics can break down defenses, which can be great if the people involved are mature enough to keep their heads. They certainly have the potential to bring people together, but they can also create all kinds of messes, too.

g2-emuB.text:
There is another reason for what I've seen. If people are attracted to the revelatory aspect of psychedelic spirituality and don't want the hard work, then in the absence of any other mode of community organization, they will eventually try to make the psychedelic use the keystone of how their community operates. But if they don't have the basic social skills to work together on a rational plane then it's a nonstarter.

Yes, I think that there are also very good arguments for the use of psychedelics in a communal setting. I have seen them both greatly enhance interpersonal relationships by getting people out of the ruts of their normal negative interaction patterns, and greatly confuse and mess things up. It depends a lot on how mature a group is to begin with.

g3-emuA.text:
The downloads you experience will be able to be put into perspective more easily by other people who have done it before. Psychedelics have a habit of making it seem like everything you think is incredibly insightful and brand new, even if it is complete bullshit. It can be nice to have some friends who can tell the difference.

It’s easier to establish a pattern/ceremony of use. Most “traditional” drug use is done in a communal setting where ceremonies are timed appropriately and there’s less of a compulsion to constantly take the substance over and over again.

g3-emuB.text:
The people around you can help keep you grounded and reality test your experience during your downloads. Psychedelics can give you true insight and meaning and they can also give you complete nonsense with the same bright shining light. Having people around who know you might help you tell the difference between what is useful and what is fluff.

Community helps keep you in rhythm. Many traditional ceremonies use this modality. It keeps you from using too often out of compulsion and gives you time to integrate when you do use.

g4-emuA.text:
To clarify, I do not believe that there needs to be special “shamans.” I know this goes against a lot of traditional lineages, including many ayahuasca and Bwiti lineages. It is not my intention to devalue the work of others.

The reason I say this, is because I think that it can lead to problems when people in a vulnerable state put their faith in a single charismatic individual. If these individuals are floating around on the retreat circuit, they may or may not have been vetted by any other authorities, if such exist, and may or may not be held accountable by any given group. When someone is deeply open, these people may or may not be taking advantage of them, sexually or in other ways (the need for repeat business, for example). Or they may simply be wrong.

g4-emuB.text:
To clarify, I don’t think there need to be ‘shamans’ in a particular way. I realize this may not be the traditional view, and many people in ayahuasca / bwiti lineages disagree with me on this, but I do think it’s important.

There shouldn’t be charismatic leaders to blindly follow. The person running the retreat that one happens to join while traveling around the world doing retreats may or may not be wise, is likely to not be well vetted or held accountable, could be sexually abusive, profits from one returning to them, and could easily be wrong about things, especially given how open one is in these states.

g5-emuA.text: I'm not clear how a culture of peer-led medicine prevents the emergence of a "shaman" - a person that everyone is looking to for information and guidance, a person that is trusted without question. Just because the role is temporary and there is public accountability, I'm not sure that it would prevent that kind of dynamic from emerging.

g5-emuB.text: I don't see how a culture of peer-led medicine prevents someone from becoming the de facto shaman of a community. I suppose rotating the position and holding the person publically accountable for their actions might help, but I don't think it would fully prevent it.

g6-emuA.text: Peer led does not mean careless. A certain amount of screening for medical and psychiatric contra-indications is necessary. Being aware of medications and the effects of combining them is important. Having a sober sitter, preferably someone qualified to recognize when to call for professional or emergency services, is needed. Because authority is distributed, more people need to be competent.

g6-emuB.text: It seems that there is some confusion about what "peer-led" means in this context. Peer-led does not mean that there are no precautions taken in terms of screening for medical or psychiatric contraindications, checking what medications people are on and what combinations might be problematic, providing a sober sitter who is appropriate for the situation, knowing when a situation requires professional intervention or even emergency care, etc. In fact, because authority is distributed, a higher level of competence is needed.

g7-emuA.text:
This is one of the many reasons that the medicine comes after a lot of other pl/ork. Things like reparenting, developing somatic capacity, peer counseling, etc. are needed first, as medicine can only enhance what’s already there. It cannot, by pharmacological fiat, create integration.

This, also, has the benefit of screening out those whose main interest is in collecting experiences. If they’re unwilling to do the 6 month pre-req of learning how to listen, then they’re not going to magically get better at it just because they saw some cool looking visions.

The real integration comes in how one lives their life AFTER the ceremony.

g7-emuB.text:
The medicine will wait for them behind the other pl/ork. Reparenting, somatic capacity, peer counsel, etc etc need to come first, for a variety of reasons. One of them is that medicine cannot replace these things, it can only enhance what’s already there.

Two is that this is a necessary experience to weed out the experience collectors who won’t invest 6 months in growing their relational skills and therefore are unlikely to benefit from increasing their relational maturity as a result of whatever geometry they saw in their visions.

Three is that integration is the outside life between ceremonies.
